title: A Tibetan day

cards: Early morning in a Tibetan settlement in India. A grandmother wakes before her family, washes her face, and fills seven small bowls with water on the family shrine. She lights a lamp and bows three times.

Then she walks to the temple with her beads, joining a slow river of people circling it clockwise, murmuring, turning the prayer wheels as they pass. Later she'll sit for a while at home. None of it is dramatic.
All of it has a shape.

teach.b: Tibetan teachers often say a practice should be good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end.
It begins with refuge: turning toward the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and in Tibetan practice often the teacher too. Right after comes bodhicitta, the reminder of why: for all beings.
Many people say a short traditional verse joining the two, three times.
The middle is the practice itself: om mani padme hum on the beads, a praise to Tara, a visualization, or tonglen, riding the breath. Whatever it is, teachers say to do it without grabbing at results.
Whatever good came from this is given away, to all beings, so it can't turn into a private trophy. A ten-minute session and a three-year retreat share that same shape.

teach.h: WATER BOWLS, LAMPS, THE TEMPLE WALK.
teach.b: Around it sits the rest of the day: water bowls and lamps, the walk around the temple, the wheels, the flags on the roof. Now look back at two weeks on the roof of the world.
The diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it.
Turn the mind. Check the teacher. Take in, send out.
One slogan. For all of us. She comes quickly.
Swept away. Four streams. Carried into exile.
In between. And today, the diamond day. Tomorrow the path comes down from the mountains, to wherever you live, with a practical question: who will you practice with?

how: Tibetan Buddhists often begin the day with water-bowl offerings and prostrations, circle temples and stupas clockwise with prayer beads, and shape each practice session with refuge and bodhicitta at the start and a dedication of merit at the end.

o: a festival day on the lunar calendar
a day shaped by refuge, practice and dedication
a day of silence kept once a year by monks

games.q: match each part of the Tibetan day.

s: Tibetan practice sessions usually end by dedicating the merit to all beings
that way the good can't turn into a private trophy.
Tibetan Buddhists circle a temple counterclockwise
they walk clockwise, keeping the temple on their right.
a three-year retreat has a different shape from a ten-minute session
teachers say both are good in the beginning, middle and end.

games.q: you've just finished a good sit and feel great. a Tibetan teacher would say there's one more step. what is it?
o: write down how good it felt.
dedicate whatever good came from it to all beings.
sit longer to keep the feeling.
games.why: the session ends with dedication: the good is given away to all beings, which completes the shape.

practice: Here's the shape in miniature: begin by turning silently toward what you take refuge in, and remember you're not sitting only for yourself.
In the middle, sit with the breath, or murmur om mani padme hum if that feels right, without chasing any result.
At the end, give it away, whatever good came from this, for all beings; another day, the same shape can stretch to fifteen minutes.

wordCard.voice: A Tibetan day. Refuge and bodhicitta at the start, mantra or tonglen in the middle, and dedication at the end: good in the beginning, middle and end.

orig.note: Sanskrit pariṇāmanā: dedication, turning the merit of practice toward the good of all beings. Tibetan: ngowa.

carryVoice: Your line: the diamond day. Good in the beginning, the middle and the end. Two weeks on the mountain, complete.
